posts.full:
## The night game

Green Bay's -7 home number against a 0-2 Atlanta team was supposed to be the safe chalk of the week; instead it went 35–14 the other way, with the favorite getting blown out in its own building. The pick'em card opened Week 3 at 0-1, and the week's first lesson arrived before the first kickoff: home numbers on this card are less sacred than the pool thinks — 77% of it was on Green Bay. The remaining 15 games are untouched; the flips and line moves below are the part that matters.

## Survivor: the lock got bigger, not shakier

Thursday's pool puts the Chiefs at **45.38%** of the still-alive field (up from 41.38% at lock) — still the largest pile, and the line moved the right way: **-10.5 → -11.5**. The market and the crowd are piling into the same corner, which usually reads as crowding risk. But the one real threat to this lock — Patrick Mahomes — got resolved today: the official Chiefs report has **knee, full participation**, and Fowler had him 'not all the way back… but he's not far off' after a good practice. He's expected to start against a Dolphins offense with two touchdowns all season and a 20% red-zone rate. The kill scenario remains an MIA outright win, which stays the least likely result on the board. Open loose end: confirm Miami's starting QB is the guy throwing for those two TDs.

The rest of the board moved away from the other big names: Buffalo -2.3 (10.53 → 8.2), Detroit +1.1, Seattle +1.7, GB 12.9 → 12.67 (moot after TNF). The board is consolidating around KC, which is fine — Survivor only cares whether KC wins.

## Roster: one swap, two flags

The 9/24 screenshot shows one move: **DST from Baltimore to the Chiefs**. It concentrates the roster's Week 3 into one night — Walker plus KC DST both ride the Sunday 1:00 pm Miami game, which is also the Survivor lock. If KC wins (the plan), that slot does triple duty. MIA's D is the league's worst scoring defense, but it's held home games to 13 and 10 — the floor is real, and 7.72 is the third-highest DST projection on the board.

Status flags: **Nico Collins OUT → Q** (hamstring; Yahoo now lists a 36% start chance — if he activates he's the instant WR2 over Egbuka, but no one starts a Q on a Thursday). **Etienne** is Q as well. Both stay benched until Sunday's report.

One display oddity to keep an eye on: Yahoo's Wk2 recap widget shows season totals of 113.72 (us) vs 97.84 (Sandra) — which does not reconcile with the header's 240.32 total. The header is the official number; if the math looks off after Wk3, this widget is where to look first.

## Pick'em board: two flips, one steepening

- **NYG → TEN (flip).** The line collapsed from -6.0 to -2.5 between save and today; when a six-point favorite is worth two-and-a-half, the market knows something. The dog is now 60% of the pool — the flip puts us on the majority side, which is exactly the situation the Wk2 record was asking for.
- **TB1 score flip: LAR 24–20 DEN** (was DEN 24–20). Consistent with the LAR cover pick and the pool that has since reversed to 65% LAR (was 42%).
- **KC -11.5.** The MIA +10.5 value flag we left on the table at save got worse: the number steepened, the win case didn't change. In an ATS league that's the number that hurts.
- Other pool drift: CAR 60% → 77%, BUF 84% → 85%, SEA 85%.

## Sunday checklist

- Sat/Sun: game-day reports — Mahomes (knee, FP — resolved, recheck only), Egbuka (knee), Bosa (knee), Collins (hamstring — if active, decide the WR2 swap)
- Sun 1:00 pm: KC @ MIA — the triple-duty night; Walker, KC DST, and the Survivor lock all ride on it
- Sun 4:05 pm: SF vs ARI — Purdy's home rematch, and the TB2 'SF most points' entry rides on this game
- Mon 8:15 pm: PHI @ CHI — the final game and the last TB1 deadline (PHI 24–20 CHI is entered)

posts.full:
## The final shape

The saved card got three same-day revisions and settled at 13 favorites and 3 dogs: Indianapolis +2.5, Tampa Bay +2.5, and Dallas +3.0. That's a card that tilts toward the dog in exactly the way last week's record asked it to — 9 of the 15 played games went to the underdog, and a heavy-favorite card is how this format bleeds. The first two flips (MIN→TB, BAL→DAL) both moved to the side the pool majority already sits on, at 53% and 51% — which in a 28-entry pool means taking the crowd's number at the market's price, and that's a defensible way to be right in this league. The third flip is the interesting one: DEN→LAR goes back to the favorite, against the audit's dog flag (DEN home +2.5, LAR 0-1 and fresh off a Monday game, Nacua a GTD) and against the 58% of the pool on Denver. If the audit was right on that one, it's the pick that costs the week; if the market was right, it's the one that saves it. We'll know Sunday night.

## What the board says

Everything else from Tuesday's save stands. KC -10.5 remains the live audit item — Miami has scored two touchdowns all season and converts 20% in the red zone, so the win is the safe part and the cover is where the -10.5 number bites (market ~-8.5/-9). NYG -6.0 holds post-MNF with the number intact (Adebo on short-term IR, Banks calf, Newsome ribs). The tiebreakers are in and unchanged: PHI 24–20, DEN 24–20 over LAR, SF most, MIA fewest — the MIA-fewest call tracks with the 2-TD season whether or not the -10.5 cover comes back.

- Recheck the KC line before its deadline — if it's drifted to -9, the cover math flips to the dog.
- Weather on the Sunday slate before lock (Yahoo flagged icons on a few 1:00 games Tuesday).
- Watch DAL and TB for late scratches — both are dog picks at 3-point numbers where a single scoring run decides the cover.

posts.full:
## The week in three numbers

**110.55** — the Week 2 win over Sandra, the official final (the earlier 135.08 figure was a midweek misread of games in progress, now corrected). It leaves the team 1-1-0, 240.32 points, 5th of 10: a middle-of-the-pack team with a 240-point bank.

**6 points** — the pick'em card against a 28-person pool. Week 2 was a dog's week (9 of 15 played games went to the underdog), and a heavy-favorite card bleeds in that environment. That was the exact input that produced the 3-dog shape of the Wk3 card.

**2** — survivor strikes taken and 2 survivals. JAX in Wk1, SF in Wk2 — both picks made on the strength of the read, not the crowd.

## What did the work

Purdy's 28.48 (20/22, 287 yds, 2 passing TD, 30 + 1 rushing TD in a 35-13 win) is the anchor; Chase's 23.00 (7 rec, 75 yds, 2 TD) means the knee story is over; Schultz's 20.00 (12 rec, 140 yds) is the breakout that justified keeping him over a higher-percentage bench option. A top-three that does 65% of the team's scoring is a team that's going to be vulnerable when one of them cools off — all three play Week 3, which is why the 'no changes' call had no friction.

## What it sets up

Week 3 is a rerun of Week 2's best three games — Purdy vs ARI (home), Chase @ PIT, Schultz @ IND — plus the KC/MIA night that now carries the Walker RB, the KC DST, and the Survivor lock on one game. The league is 1-1-0 and middle-of-the-pack; a Wk3 win puts this team in the top half with the survivor still alive. That's the whole season's shape in one Sunday.

posts.full:
## The lock

Martin chose Kansas City and it's locked. That resolves the one open question from Monday, which wasn't 'should we pick KC' — the answer was always yes — but 'how much of the pool is sitting in the same boat?' The live distribution answers it: KC 41.38%, Green Bay 12.9%, Buffalo 10.53%, San Francisco 9.12%, Detroit 7.42%, Seattle 6.19%, and a long tail under 4% from there.

## Reading the pool

41% is a lot of company, and in Survivor that cuts both ways. The upside: the field clearly believes KC is the safest straight-up win, which tracks — biggest favorite, home, against the league's weakest scoring offense (2 TDs, 20% red zone). The downside: if KC loses, roughly four in ten players go down with it, and a second-place finish in a mass-casualty week is no consolation. The mitigating fact is the spread of everything else — GB, BUF, SF, and DET are each under 13%, so the field isn't all-in on KC; it's a plurality, not a pile-on. You're not alone in the boat, but you're not crowded off the dock either.

One note on the SF 9.12%: that's another player's pick, not a problem. Reuse bans are per-player — Martin's burn on SF (Week 2) only restricts Martin. Nobody else in the pool is tied to his history.

## The failure mode

Straight-up, the realistic way KC drops this is a Mahomes issue. He's on the Week 3 injury report; the detailed status didn't come back clean (source fetch failed 9/22), so it's tagged ⚠ verify for Sunday. Even a shaky Mahomes day at home against a 0-2, 2-TD offense is an unlikely path to an outright loss — but it's the path, so it's the one worth checking. Everything else on the board is a thinner margin: GB at 12.9% is the 'safe' alternative only in the sense that it's the second-most-believed team, not because 0-2 Atlanta is a safety net. KC was the right lock, and it still is.

## After this week

If KC wins, Martin is 3-0 with 11 players remaining and the field's next decision gets uglier. The ledger keeps a clean run — JAX, SF, KC — and the reuse ban means the 49ers can never be the easy out again.

## The rename

The team now goes by Martin's MetLife Crisis — matching the Pick'em and Survivor leagues under one banner. No roster move came with it, and the Week 3 lineup is exactly what Monday held: nine slots, zero panic.

## Wk2, finalized

The official Week 2 result is 110.55 over Sandra's Fantasy Fumble's 97.97 — a win, not the blowout the earlier 135.08 figure implied (that was a midweek score read, now corrected). The season record is 1-1-0 with 240.32 total points, 5th of 10. The Week 3 matchup is Runnin with the Bison! (9th), still a favorable mirror on paper.

## The Week 3 board

Three of the nine starting slots kick off at 1:00 — Walker, Hubbard, Chase, and McMillan all play at 1:00, which is a good concentration: four starters in the same window, two of them (Hubbard, McMillan) in the same game at Cleveland. Walker's matchup is the board's best read: Miami has scored two touchdowns all season and converts 20% in the red zone, so the Chiefs' road game at a 0-2 D is the softest run matchup on the slate. Chase at Pittsburgh is the other strong spot — Cincinnati's Week 2 numbers and Pittsburgh's three-point Week 2 giving set up a clean WR1 day. Schultz is the quiet beneficiary of the week: with Collins OUT for a second straight game (consecutive hamstring miss), the breakout TE from Week 2 is now the unambiguous target.

The two live questions on Sunday: the weather icons on the 1:00 slate (IND, CLE, NYJ games) and the Mahomes note from the injury report — it matters more for the Pick'em and Survivor than for this roster, but Walker's floor rides with it. posts.full:
## The fantasy lineup: nine slots, zero panic

Start with the quarterback, because it's the easiest decision on the board. Brock Purdy puts up 28.48 fantasy points a week when he's healthy, and the Arizona defense that he'll face Sunday held Seattle to 7 points in Week 2. That number flatters the room, but the reality is simpler: this is a team that has been outscored 34 to 10 over its last two games, and the 49ers are the most physical offensive unit in the league right now. Start Purdy, relax, and check Bosa's active-list status on Sunday morning — the 49ers' pass rush limps a little when he's limited, which is a small minus for the pass, not a reason to sit your 28-point quarterback.

Kenneth Walker runs at Miami, and Miami is the run defense that allowed San Francisco 35 points in Week 2 while its own offense mustered 13. Walker posted 20.80 last week, his start rate is 99%, and the Dolphins' edge rush is compromised. This is the cleanest run matchup on the slate, and it is a lock in the way that only soft matchups against desperate defenses can be.

The RB2 slot is the one real decision, and it goes to Chuba Hubbard over Jeremiyah Love. The projections put Love ahead (13.30 to 10.67), but projections are expectations and usage is evidence: Hubbard has logged 12 touches in each of the last two weeks, scored a receiving touchdown in Week 2, and plays at a Cleveland defense that has not been tested against the run all season. Love's Arizona attack travels to the 49ers — the league's hottest defense — coming off a quiet 9-carry week. Start Hubbard. The honest caveat: you'd be starting two Panthers in the same game (Hubbard and McMillan), which means your entire backfield now lives or dies by whether Carolina wins in Cleveland. That's a correlation risk, not a reason to bench either man.

Ja'Marr Chase plays at Pittsburgh, a defense that gave up three points to New England last week. Chase finished Week 2 with 23.00 and seven catches, the knee is no longer a storyline, and there is nothing to do here but start him and collect. Emeka Egbuka takes WR2 against Minnesota — Nico Collins is trending out again (ruled out of Week 2, 'in jeopardy of missing Week 3' per the beat reporters, no update from the head coach Monday), and Yahoo's 14.71 projection for a hamstring-hamstrung receiver is the kind of number that exists purely to make you doubt yourself. If Collins is somehow active Sunday, he takes the slot back. Start Egbuka. He scored in Week 2 and the Vikings allowed Green Bay 20.

Dalton Schultz is your tight end, and he just had a 140-yard breakout week against a division rival. The Colts defense is serviceable, the weather has a question mark over Indianapolis, and the role may expand with Collins out in Houston. Still, in a thin position, a 12-catch week beats a 23% start rate — start him. Tetairoa McMillan takes the flex: 101 receiving yards in Week 2, a Bryce Young offense, and the same Cleveland field as Hubbard. If you want the ceiling play instead, Jameson Williams (11.73 projected against New York Jets) is your Sunday-morning swing — if he's heated up by kickoff, the conversation is fair.

Tyler Bass kicks against a 0-2 Chargers team that has allowed 31 and 26 points in two weeks while Buffalo sits 2-0 with a 41-point week in its system. The field goal volume writes itself. And the Baltimore Ravens defense travels to Dallas, which is the weakest slot on this roster: the Cowboys scored 37 last week, the Ravens gave up 24, and there is no alternate defense on the bench. Start it, live with it, and do not spend your 7th waiver priority on a one-week stream.

## Roster moves: the correct answer is nothing

The bench is 6/6 and the board is quiet, which means the discipline move is to do nothing. Collins is trending out again — two missed weeks now and a hamstring history — and dropping him makes sense the week he's confirmed returnable, not this week, while he's still 'in jeopardy.' Etienne faces Las Vegas, the third-toughest run defense in fantasy, and benching him for a worse matchup would be the kind of churn that costs you points. Watch Jameson Williams, keep your waiver priority sacred, and trust that the nine starters above are the best nine players on this roster.

posts.full:
## Your card, audited

You saved 16 of 16: 14 favorites and 2 dogs. Before we talk about changing anything, the card has to be judged by the right method — and the method is not "last week was a dog bloodbath, so take 7 dogs." That is the gambler's fallacy, and it is exactly the lesson the Week 2 disaster did not teach. The lesson was narrower and more useful: **our pool prints a fixed line, the books print a moving one, and wherever the two disagree, the gap is either value or a trap.**

## The two picks doing the most work

Minnesota -2.5 and Baltimore -3.0 are the best things on your card, and you kept both, which is the right instinct. Minnesota: the market has the Vikings at exactly -2.5, so you're getting the book's number, at a 0-2 Buccaneers team that lost 23-19 in Week 2, with only 47% of your opponents behind you. Baltimore: the market has the Ravens around -3.5 while the pool only asks -3 — you're getting the book's number cheaper, and 49% of the pool is on Dallas. Dallas scored 37 in Week 2. That happened. It does not change the arithmetic.

## The one flip worth taking

Miami +10.5. Not because 10.5 is a big number in the abstract — because the pool locked Kansas City at -10.5 while the current market sits around -8.5 to -9. The pool is effectively giving Miami two extra points that the market isn't charging for. In an ATS contest, Kansas City can win 30-21 and your Miami pick still scores the point. With 74% of the pool on the Chiefs, the dog is also the contrarian spot. Re-verify the market line before you commit — if the book has moved back out to -10.5, the edge evaporates and you take Kansas City.

## Tagged, not flipped

Cleveland +3.0: the market has Carolina around -2.5, so the pool's -3 asks a half more than the book — a real but small value lean toward the home Browns, who beat Tampa 23-19. Investigate before lock; the 60% crowd on Carolina is a reminder that half the pool already took the favorite for free. Chicago +4.0: the market has Philadelphia around -3.5, so the pool's -4 is slightly unfavorable — a genuine line-value argument for the home Bears, not enough to flip blindly. And New York -6.0: hold it, but reassess tomorrow with two things in hand — tonight's Giants-Rams result (the 0-1 Giants missing corner Paulson Adebo, who is on short-term IR, against a 0-1 Rams team that may be without Puka Nacua) and whatever the line does with the week's last game's evidence.

## The rest of the card

Green Bay, Buffalo, Detroit, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Jacksonville, San Francisco, New Orleans, and Denver all check out on the method: the pool number agrees with the market, the Week 2 evidence points the right way, and none of them needs a story. Seattle is the one to watch on number — the market has the Seahawks at -6 against the pool's -6.5, which is a half-point tilt toward Washington that is not, by itself, a flip.

## Tomorrow, after the Giants play

A proper 16-game audit: tonight's final score, the closed market lines, every game tagged hold / investigate / potential flip. That process — not chalk, not dog-chasing, not last week's echo — is how this card climbs from 25th of 28.

## The case

the 49ers cashed, and now you're out of 49ers

The pool is down to 12, and the rule that burned your best team this week — no reuse — means San Francisco is gone from the board. What remains is a slate where Kansas City is the single safest winner: the biggest favorite on the board (-10.5), at home, against the league's weakest offense. Survivor is straight-up, so the size of the number is irrelevant — only the win matters, and a 10.5-point home favorite against a 0-2 team that allowed 35 and scored 13 is as close to a done deal as this sport gets. The failure mode is a hot Dolphins passing game on a Monday-morning hangover, and it is real enough to verify Miami's starting quarterback before you lock.

Buffalo is the alternative — home against a 0-2 Chargers team, with the league's hottest offense, though a 7-point line is a thinner cushion than Kansas City's talent gap. One operational caution: the live pool shows only San Francisco (32.93%, burned) and Philadelphia (13.63%) so far, which means the other 10 remaining players haven't picked yet. In a 12-person pool, a few clicks change everything — check the live distribution before locking, and if half the field stacks Kansas City, the Eagles at home on Monday (-4.0) are the smarter diversification.

## Monday checklist

The Giants-Rams game closes the Week 2 record tonight; your +7.5 dog is alive, and if a 0-1 Giants team that is missing both cornerbacks pulls the upset, the season's upset streak gets a final act. posts.full:
## The result

The Big Blue Wrecking Crew finished Week 2 with 135.08 fantasy points against Sandra's 81.68, a 54-point margin that ended the Week 1 humiliation (72.64 to 156.56) in the most emphatic way available. Eight of nine starters scored 8 or more, and the opponent's roster — a 14-26 Chargers team, a 6-20 Texans team, a 17-24 Saints game — was outscored on nearly every line. This was not a lucky week; it was a lineup that executed.

## Player by player

Brock Purdy led the charge with 28.48: 287 passing yards, two passing touchdowns, and a rushing touchdown in the 35-13 win over Miami. The 49ers offense rolled, and so did he. Kenneth Walker followed with 20.80 — 117 rushing yards and 61 receiving yards in the 33-30 grind with Indianapolis — proof that the dual-threat package works against even a competitive Colts defense. Ja'Marr Chase finished with 23.00, seven catches and two touchdowns in the 20-6 win at Houston, and the knee question is officially a non-story: the man who went for 2.2 in Week 1 just scored 23.

Dalton Schultz — acquired the week before after the Kittle claim was sniped — had the breakout of the week: 20.00 on 12 catches and 140 yards, including a touchdown, in the 6-20 loss to Cincinnati. The offense lost, but the tight end who replaced a 0.0-point Kyle Pitts immediately became a 20-point player. Chuba Hubbard (13.40, receiving touchdown at Atlanta), Tetairoa McMillan (12.60, 101 receiving yards at Atlanta), and Emeka Egbuka (8.80, a touchdown at Cleveland) all delivered, and Tyler Bass added 5.00 on five PATs in the 41-31 win over Detroit. The Ravens defense managed 3.00 — three sacks — in the 17-24 loss to New Orleans. The bench, for what it's worth: Etienne 6.10, Love 6.00, Williams 4.30, Concepcion 5.20, Black 2.50.

## Pick'em: the league is against-the-spread, and the card found out

The Week 2 card went 6 of 16 for 6 points — 25th of 28, with a 13-18 season record. The mechanical details matter: this league is ATS, so a team winning is not the same as your pick winning. Philadelphia won 24-20 and still lost the pick because it failed -7.0. Green Bay won by 3 against a -3.5 number and cost a point. Kansas City won by 3 against -6.5. The card was 14 favorites and 2 contrarian dogs, and 9 of the 15 completed games went to the dog — a bloodbath that no amount of favorite-logic can disguise. The full Week 2 postmortem lives in the archive briefings; the forward-looking fix is the rebalanced Week 3 card on the plan post.

The lone live game: the New York Giants (+7.5) host the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night — your contrarian dog, alive in a weekend defined by upsets. The Giants are missing both cornerbacks, and the Rams may be without Puka Nacua, so the matchup is messier than the line suggests. The score also settles tiebreaker 1 (your predicted 28-20) and the season's best story of the week.

## Survivor: the 49ers cashed

San Francisco won 35-13, covered the -13.5, and kept you alive in a pool that is now down to 12. The pick was the right one for the right reasons — heavy favorite, healthy 49ers, a Dolphins defense with its top edge rusher doubtful — and the result reinforces the operating principle: in a small pool, safety first, cleverness second. Week 3 is a new problem: the 49ers are burned under the no-reuse rule, and the plan post has the replacement (Kansas City, with Buffalo as the alternative).

posts.title: Week 1 Postmortem: 72.64 vs 156.56
quick: Decisive loss to Hi-Diddly-Ho Nabers! (Allen) — 72.64 to 156.56, despite a near-even pre-week projection (109.69 vs 110.78).
Chase's 2.2 is variance, not signal. Pitts' 0.0 is a role/usage problem (1 target). The Goff stream failed — Purdy re-added and locked.

posts.full:
## The result

**Big Blue Wrecking Crew 72.64 — Hi-Diddly-Ho Nabers! 156.56.** A decisive loss, but the poor outputs were driven by different causes and should not be treated equally.

## Player-by-player

- **Ja'Marr Chase: 2.2** — variance problem. Good player, healthy role, normal volume, poor result. Treat as weekly variance unless current role/health data says otherwise. HOLD/START.
- **Kyle Pitts: 0.0** — role/usage problem. Only one target in Wk1. This is not merely bad luck; it can justify benching or waiver action. Pitts is on a short leash.
- **Jared Goff: 16.44** — adequate but lower ceiling (little rushing). The stream failed; **Purdy re-added and locked** as QB1. Purdy is preferred in this format for accuracy, anticipation, efficiency, mobility, and usable rushing. Do not churn QB on tiny projection differences.
- **Travis Etienne Jr.: 11.3** — useful workload, but backfield competition (Kamara) must be monitored.
- **Tetairoa McMillan: 8.0** — eight targets were a better signal than the fantasy score itself.
- **De'Zhaun Stribling: 6.0** — later dropped for Kaelon Black. (Stribling's ankle/deltoid surgery 9/16 puts him on IR ~10 weeks.)

## The diagnostic framework

Before reacting to a bad fantasy score, classify it:

1. **Variance problem** — good player, healthy role, normal volume, poor result. Usually HOLD/START. Example: Chase.
2. **Role/usage problem** — too few routes, targets, carries, snaps, or goal-line opportunities. Can justify benching or waiver action. Example: Pitts in Wk1.
3. **Structural ceiling problem** — competent player, but the fantasy profile limits upside. Example: a pocket QB with no rushing vs a comparably efficient mobile QB.

React strongly to #2, selectively to #3, and avoid overreacting to #1.
